cooperbench.notes:
The benchmark exists: it is CooperBench, arXiv 2601.13295.

How I read it
- arxiv.org, cooperbench.com, iclr.cc, openreview.net and huggingface.co are all blocked by this session's network policy, for both curl and WebFetch. I did not try to get around that.
- I read the paper from the authors' own PDF in their public website repository, cooperbench/website at commit 97dbb0a, file public/static/pdfs/main.pdf. It is 33 pages, its header is dated 2026-1-27, and its title matches the arXiv citation in the code repository.
- The code repository is cooperbench/CooperBench, cloned at commit 63b9d44 (2026-09-14). I treated both clones as data and ran none of their code.
- Quotes from the PDF come from pdftotext. I collapsed whitespace and line breaks, rejoined words split by hyphens across lines, and dropped footnote markers. For example, the 100-action sentence has a footnote marker "2" after "(100)". Quotes from table rows are whitespace-normalised.
- I rendered the Fig. 4 bar values (page 7) as an image and checked them against Table 5. The counts divided by 652 match the bars.

Not verified
- ICLR 2026 acceptance. A search result lists "CooperBench: Benchmarking Cooperation in Coding Agents" at iclr.cc/virtual/2026/10018462, but I could not open that page. Neither repository mentions ICLR. Treat the venue as unconfirmed.
- The arXiv version history and submission date. The id prefix 2601 only means January 2026.

Internal inconsistencies in the paper
- The headline gap: "30% lower" in the abstract, "around 50%" or "roughly half" in the introduction and conclusion, and "41% lost, retention 0.59" in Appendix C.
- The number of pools: 34, 32 (the actual sum of Table 3) and 52, against 30 in the dataset.
- The merge resolver: "Qwen 3 Coder 1.5B" in the main text, "Qwen2.5-Coder-0.5B-Instruct" in Appendix B.
- Gold conflict rate: 77.3% in the paper, 76.5% in the current dataset.

What this means for the planned experiment
1. CooperBench's Coop arm is already the pull-request-gated, multi-developer workflow: separate branches, no shared view of the code, text messages only, one merge at the end. That arm is the one that lost to Solo. The paper never tests a shared workspace. It does not show that too much collaboration hurts; it shows that coordinating under workspace isolation with messages only does worse than one agent doing both features.
2. The volume of communication did not matter: with-comm against no-comm was not significant. The closest result to "more collaborators hurts" is the 2-to-4-agent run on 46 tasks, with the model unnamed.
3. The authors' own later ablation points the other way from the user's hypothesis, though it is small (one seed, n=50, codex/gpt-5.5). Agents that share code through a git remote or a shared scratchpad and task list beat Solo (56% and 62% against 48%); messaging-only isolation is worst at 26%.
4. The paper measures success only: no time, tokens or cost. A claim about productivity needs new metrics.
5. Results depend heavily on the merge policy. Under the paper's policy, union merge adds about 6-15 points to Coop. The current harness drops union merge and the resolver and falls back to the lead's patch alone. Fix the merge policy and the dataset version before comparing any arm with the paper.
6. The Solo agent in the paper has a 100-action cap, the same as each Coop agent, so the two Coop agents get twice the total budget. Budget parity is a design choice to make on purpose.
7. A Claude Code adapter already exists in the repository, which could serve as the harness.

Nearest related work the paper cites (not opened): Davidson et al. 2025, "The Collaboration Gap", arXiv 2511.02687; Su et al. 2025, cited for 39-70% multi-agent degradation; Cemri et al. 2025, "Why do multi-agent LLM systems fail?", arXiv 2503.13657.

claims.claim: The paper text read here is the authors' own PDF from their website repository (33 pages). Its header is dated 2026-1-27 and it carries the same title. arXiv itself could not be opened from this session, so it is not confirmed whether this PDF matches every arXiv version.
claims.quote: 2026-1-27 ... CooperBench: Why Coding Agents Cannot be Your Teammates Yet

claims.claim: A task is one repository state plus two features, each with its own hidden unit tests. Each agent sees only its own feature. Tasks are every pair of features drawn from a feature pool built on one base commit.
claims.quote: Each task consists of a repository state, two features, and two corresponding sets of unit tests. The two features are drawn from a pool of features (like the one illustrated in Fig. 2) that can be simultaneously implemented on the given repository state. The patches from the two agents are merged and evaluated. ... Note that agents can only view their own features.

claims.claim: Scale: 652 tasks from 12 repositories in 4 languages (Python, TypeScript, Go, Rust). There are 199 features. Nine of the twelve repositories are Python.
claims.quote: CooperBench comprises 652 tasks constructed from 12 popular open-source libraries across Python, TypeScript, Go, and Rust.

claims.claim: The paper contradicts itself on how many feature pools there are: 34 in section 2.1, a Table 3 column that adds up to 32 while printing 34, and 52 in Appendix A.2. The repository's dataset has 30 task directories (pools). Their pairs add up to 652 and their features to 199 (my count). The pool count matters as the cluster unit for confidence intervals.
claims.quote: In CooperBench we have 34 such features pools. ... The final CooperBench benchmark comprises 199 individual features grouped into 52 task sets, yielding 652 evaluated feature pairs.

claims.claim: Conflict is built in. The paper says 77.3% of tasks have gold solutions that conflict. The repository's current report says naive git merge of the two gold patches conflicts on 499 of 652 pairs (76.5%). One combined.patch per pool implements every feature and is the resolved oracle.
claims.quote: so `git merge` of `feature1.patch` and `feature2.patch` conflicts for 499 of the 652 pairs (see `gold_conflict_report.json`). That is the coordination challenge the benchmark measures, not a defect

claims.claim: Each agent works in its own isolated workspace (a separate VM or Docker container on its own branch). Neither can see the other's code. The two patches are merged only once, after both agents finish.
claims.quote: In our benchmarking process, we use cloud virtual machines for agents to ensure isolated workspaces and sufficient resources. ... After the two agents complete execution, we attempt to merge their resulting patches using git merge-file -L patch_1 -L repo_state -L patch_2.

claims.claim: The only channel between agents is free-text messages through a send tool, which the paper's harness backed with an SQL database. A message lands in the recipient's prompt on its next step. Agents act asynchronously and do not take turns. Each agent is capped at 100 actions, and messages count against that cap. Tools are limited to local file and terminal operations. The paper states no limit on message length or count.
claims.quote: When an agent sends a message to another agent, the other agent will immediately receive it, and include it in the prompt of the next step. This communication setting achieves both real-time communication and asynchronous execution.

claims.claim: The paper's runs set a 100-action cap per agent. The authors say a higher cap did not help.
claims.quote: We set an upper-bound number (100) of actions an agent can take to complete the tasks.

claims.claim: The paper compares these arms: Solo (one agent implements both features), Coop with communication (two agents, one feature each), and Coop with no communication (messaging tool banned). A small extra experiment scales to 3 and 4 agents.
claims.quote: In CooperBench, each of the two agents are assigned a feature to implement, which will be called the Coop setting to distinguish from the Solo baseline. In the Solo baseline, the two tasks are assigned to one agent.

claims.claim: Success means the two patches merge and the merged code passes both features' test suites. Merging tries a naive git merge, then a union merge, then a small learned conflict resolver. If no conflict-free patch comes out, both agents fail the task. Agents may split the work differently, as long as the merged patch implements both features.
claims.quote: If even the coding model cannot produce a patch without conflicts, the agents both fail the tasks. Implementation correctness If we successfully merge the two patches into the repository state, we run both sets of unit tests on the merged codebase.

claims.claim: Union merge accounts for a large share of the paper's Coop success. With communication, GPT-5 scores 20.42% under naive merge only, 26.64% after union and 27.90% after the learned resolver. Communication raises naive-merge success, but the gain is gone after union and resolver.
Five models were tested inside an OpenHands v0.54-based framework: GPT-5, Claude Sonnet 4.5, MiniMax-M2, Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B-Instruct and Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507.

claims.claim: The paper states its headline gap three different ways. The abstract says 30% lower on average. The introduction and conclusion say about 50% lower, or roughly half, for GPT-5 and Claude. Appendix C says 41% of Solo capability is lost. From Table 5 the per-model relative drops are about 27-61%, and the absolute drops are 1.7-22 points.
claims.quote: agents achieve on average 30% lower success rates when working together compared to performing both tasks individually, across the full spectrum of task difficulties.

claims.claim: The introduction gives the version of the headline most often cited: GPT-5 and Claude Sonnet 4.5 reach about 25% in Coop, around 50% below Solo.
claims.quote: GPT-5 and Claude Sonnet 4.5 based agents achieve only 25% with two-agent cooperation on CooperBench, which is around 50% lower than a "Solo" baseline which uses one agent to implement both features.

claims.claim: The gap between Solo and Coop is largest on tasks of middle difficulty.
claims.quote: the gap between the two settings is larger and more significant on the tasks with middle-level technical difficulty than on the ones which are too easy or too hard.

claims.claim: Adding agents lowers success: 68.6% with 2, 46.5% with 3 and 30.0% with 4. This was a small run on 46 tasks from 3 task sets, and the paper does not name the model.
claims.quote: Specifically, performance drops from 68.6% with 2 agents to 46.5% with 3 agents and further to 30.0% with 4 agents on the tasks, reinforcing the "curse of coordination" beyond the 2-agent setting.

claims.claim: Communication neither helps nor hurts success. The difference between with-comm and no-comm is not significant. Communication does cut merge conflicts, and it takes up to 20% of steps (Claude 20.0%, GPT-5 16.3%).
claims.quote: The difference between "with comm" and "no comm" settings is not statistically significant. ... This result shows that agents spent as much as 20% of the steps in communication

claims.claim: What separates useful communication: a plan in the very first turn nearly halves the conflict rate, and specific line ranges and file paths help. This fixes spatial coordination (where to edit) but not semantic coordination (what to implement).
claims.quote: Having a Plan message in the very first turn nearly halves the conflict rate (29.4% vs 51.5%).

claims.claim: Failure symptoms in Table 1 (an LLM judge labelled the failed Coop trajectories, and humans agreed on 48 of 50): work overlap 33.2%, divergent architecture 29.7%, repetition 14.7%, unresponsiveness 8.7%, unverifiable claims 4.3%, broken commitment 3.7%, and smaller categories below that.
claims.quote: Work overlap Both agents independently implement the same functionality, duplicating 33.2 work and overwriting details. Divergent architecture Incompatible design decisions lead to semantic loss even under a clean 29.7 merge.

claims.claim: Root causes in Table 2, coded by hand from 50 failed Coop traces: expectation 42%, commitment 32%, communication 26%.
claims.quote: **Expectation failures (42%)** -- agents fail to integrate partner state information - **Communication failures (26%)** -- questions go unanswered, breaking decision loops - **Commitment failures (32%)** -- agents break promises or make unverifiable claims

claims.claim: The authors trace much of the failure to workspace isolation: agents cannot check their partner's claims about code they cannot see.
claims.quote: However, collaboration under workspace isolation requires the opposite. Agents must trust partner claims about states they cannot observe.
corrections:
The claim overstates the paper. The quoted sentence is accurate, but the authors do not "trace much of the failure to workspace isolation." Workspace isolation is a fixed condition of the benchmark. The paper never varies it: there is no run with a shared workspace.

Source opened: https://github.com/cooperbench/website/blob/97dbb0aba7dd9eedf3edc92e834a9906ef474256/public/static/pdfs/main.pdf (33 pages, dated 2026-1-27).

1. The quoted passage is a hedged hypothesis, and it is about one gap only. It comes from Sec. 6.3, "The trust paradox":
"We hypothesize that a deeper tension underlies expectation failures. Models are trained to be cautious, requiring observable evidence and resisting unverifiable assertions. ... However, collaboration under workspace isolation requires the opposite. Agents must trust partner claims about states they cannot observe. When Agent A reports 'I added the handler at line 50,' Agent B's instinct is to verify, but verification fails because they are on separate branches. This mismatch between verification-first training and trust-requiring collaboration may partly explain why agents consistently fail to update their model of partner state despite explicit communication."
So the suggested cause is a mismatch between how models are trained and the trust that collaboration needs. The authors say it "may partly explain" one gap, expectation failures. They do not say isolation causes most failures.

2. The paper's own causal account names agent capability gaps, not isolation.
- Conclusion: "This curse of coordination stems from three capability gaps: agents fail to communicate actionable information, deviate from their own commitments, and hold incorrect expectations about their partners."
- Table 2 splits the causes as Expectation 42%, Commitment 32% and Communication 26%.
- Sec. 7: the results point "to social intelligence as the bottleneck for effective agent teamwork."

3. Isolation appears as context, not as the cause.
- Sec. 6.3: "The common thread is partial observability. Each agent acts while holding an uncertain model of its partner's state, edits, and commitments." The paper then says coordination "requires verifiable and actionable constraints for a partner operating under isolation." The fault it identifies is that agents do not create checkable commitments.
- The failure taxonomy's prompt says: "Do not label state mismatch or visibility confusion itself as an error (e.g., agents on separate branches unable to see each other's changes)."

4. The symptom closest to the claim is small. In Table 1, "Unverifiable claims" is 4.3% of failures and "Broken commitment" is 3.7%. The largest symptoms are "Work overlap" at 33.2% and "Divergent architecture" at 29.7%.

5. The authors' remedy is to work within isolation, not remove it. They call for "lightweight mechanisms that turn conversation into verifiable shared state, such as pasted signatures, explicit insertion-point contracts, and integration checks before declaring safety." Their future work lists "training objectives that reward coordination under partial observability" and "lightweight protocols for verifiable commitments."

Correct statement: CooperBench attributes the drop from Solo to Coop to coordination capability gaps (expectation 42%, commitment 32%, communication 26%) and to a lack of social intelligence. All of this happens under workspace isolation, which the benchmark holds fixed. The authors offer a hedged "trust paradox" hypothesis: models trained to verify, placed where they cannot see a partner's branch and must trust its claims, "may partly explain" expectation failures. The paper does not test whether isolation itself causes the failures.

This is load-bearing for the experiment design. The paper gives no evidence that a shared, visible workspace (for example, a PR-gated repo where each agent can read the other's branch) would remove the penalty. That comparison would be new evidence, not a replication of CooperBench.

Partly wrong. The paper does not trace much of the failure to workspace isolation. Workspace isolation is the setting the benchmark imposes on purpose. The authors put the failure in three capability gaps of the agents and name partial observability as the common thread. The quoted line comes from a passage the authors label as a hypothesis, and it is limited to expectation failures. Unverifiable claims, the symptom this claim describes, account for only 4.3% of failures.

Source: cooperbench/website@97dbb0a, public/static/pdfs/main.pdf (33 pages, dated 2026-1-27). I opened the PDF and extracted the text with pdftotext.

What the paper says:

1. Cause (Sec. 6, p.11): "Coordination failures stem from three capability gaps: communication (failing to exchange key information), commitment (not following through on promises), and expectation (failing to model what partners are doing)."
   - Table 2, from 50 failed Coop traces reviewed by hand: Expectation 42%, Commitment 32%, Communication 26%.
   - Conclusion (p.15): "This curse of coordination stems from three capability gaps: agents fail to communicate actionable information, deviate from their own commitments, and hold incorrect expectations about their partners."
2. Role of observability (p.12): "The common thread is partial observability. Each agent acts while holding an uncertain model of its partner's state, edits, and commitments."
3. Where the quoted line comes from (p.13): it is in "The trust paradox", which the paper presents as a hypothesis: "We hypothesize that a deeper tension underlies expectation failures. Models are trained to be cautious, requiring observable evidence and resisting unverifiable assertions... However, collaboration under workspace isolation requires the opposite. Agents must trust partner claims about states they cannot observe. When Agent A reports 'I added the handler at line 50,' Agent B's instinct is to verify, but verification fails because they are on separate branches. This mismatch between verification-first training and trust-requiring collaboration may partly explain why agents consistently fail to update their model of partner state despite explicit communication."
   - So the stated cause is a mismatch between how models are trained (verify first) and what collaboration needs (trust). It is offered as a partial explanation of expectation failures only.
4. How often unverifiable claims occur (Table 1, symptoms across all failed Coop trajectories):
   - Unverifiable claims: 4.3%.
   - Broken commitment: 3.7%.
   - Work overlap: 33.2%.
   - Divergent architecture: 29.7%.
   - Repetition: 14.7%.

Correct statement: the authors attribute the roughly 50% Coop-vs-Solo gap to agent coordination capability gaps (expectation, commitment, communication), with partial observability as the common thread. But it sits inside a hedged hypothesis, and the authors do not trace the failures to workspace isolation itself. Exact text: "The trust paradox. We hypothesize that a deeper tension underlies expectation failures. Models are trained to be cautious, requiring observable evidence and resisting unverifiable assertions. ... However, collaboration under workspace isolation requires the opposite. Agents must trust partner claims about states they cannot observe. So the mechanism the authors put forward is a mismatch: models trained to verify are placed where they have to trust. They offer it as something that "may partly explain" one cause, not as the source of "much of the failure".

- Commitment: 32%
- Communication: 26%

Related work (page 14) points "to social intelligence as the bottleneck."

Snippets claim: +80.9% for centralized coordination on parallelizable tasks; -39% to -70% for every multi-agent variant on sequential tasks; error amplification of 17.2x for independent agents vs 4.4x for centralized; diminishing or negative returns once the single-agent baseline exceeds about 45%; tool-heavy tasks hurt most. Snippet: static claim-before-write admission matched always-serial reliability (pair pass 17/14/14 vs serial 15/16/14 vs unconstrained parallel 7/6/8 out of 30), +53.3 pp pair pass over parallel; identical results on clean pairs; the dynamic-scope variant failed. (5) Gao et al., arXiv 2505.18286: the multi-agent advantage shrinks as frontier models improve.
(6) Agent-PR acceptance studies: Watanabe et al., arXiv 2509.14745 (TOSEM), 567 Claude Code PRs, reportedly 83.8% merged; AIDev, Li/Zhang/Hassan (MSR 2026, arXiv 2602.09185), reportedly agent PRs accepted less often than human PRs.
(7) Classic human software-engineering sources: Brooks's law ('adding manpower to a late software project makes it later', The Mythical Man-Month, 1975) and the human merge-conflict base rates (e.g., Ghiotto et al. TSE; Brun et al.) could not be opened. The AgenticFlict README's 'typically 10-20%' human baseline is uncited, and the same README says it has no human baseline. Do not cite Brooks or the 10-20% figure from this report.
CooperBench itself was left out as out of scope ('other evidence'). Its repository is github.com/cooperbench/CooperBench.

SYNTHESIS FOR THE EXPERIMENT:
(a) Verified evidence supports a narrower claim than the thesis. Isolation and claiming beat an unpartitioned shared workspace on coupled work: Claude Code docs, the Anthropic C compiler, and Claim Plane if verified. But no verified source shows multi-agent PR-gated work beating ONE agent working serially. harness-lab and Anthropic's own guidance point to single or serial work being as good or better at lower cost. Arms should therefore be: (i) single agent serial; (ii) N agents, isolated branches, claims, PR + CI gate; (iii) N agents in a shared workspace (agent-teams style); and ideally (iv) N independent attempts with CI selection.
(b) Match token or compute budgets across arms. Token spend explained 80% of the variance, and multi-agent setups cost 2-20x.
(c) Control task coupling: report results separately for conflict-labeled and clean work, as in the C compiler and Claim Plane.
(d) Measure the full test suite after merge, not per-PR CI, because semantic conflicts and 'poisoning' merge cleanly.
(e) Use the same model for all agents; mixed-agent pairs conflicted twice as often.
(f) Make review latency an explicit parameter. The human cost of PR gating is review wait, and an AI reviewer removes it.
(g) Choose strict up-to-date rebasing vs a merge queue on purpose, since it changes the PR arm's overhead.
(h) Keep trials isolated (no shared git history), interleave arms in time, use identical infrastructure, pre-register, and use more than 40 tasks x 3 repeats.
(i) Pick tasks near the edge of what the model can do solo; extra agents add nothing below that edge.

SOURCE-QUALITY CAVEATS: harness-lab and the Nool benchmark are not peer-reviewed; Nool is a vendor. The Anthropic C compiler and harness-design posts are n=1 engineering reports without controlled baselines. The agent-PR merge-conflict studies are 2026 preprints or SBES papers, read here through their replication packages.

claims.claim: Anthropic C-compiler project (Carlini, Feb 5, 2026): 16 Opus 4.6 agents, each in its own container clone, pushed to a shared bare git upstream. Each claimed a task by committing a lock file to current_tasks/, and git refused a second claim of the same task. This is close to this template's claim-by-first-push protocol.
claims.quote: If two agents try to claim the same task, git's synchronization forces the second agent to pick a different one.
corrections:
Partly refuted, and only on two points. Most of the claim checks out against https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/building-c-compiler, which I opened and read in full. The two points: the source does not say git "refused" a second claim, and the comparison to this template only holds for how tasks are claimed.

What the page supports, quoted exactly:
- Date, model and author: "Published Feb 05, 2026"; "We tasked Opus 4.6 using agent teams to build a C Compiler"; "Written by Nicholas Carlini, a researcher on our Safeguards team."
- Agent count: "I tasked 16 agents with writing a Rust-based C compiler, from scratch, capable of compiling the Linux kernel."
- Setup: "A new bare git repo is created, and for each agent, a Docker container is spun up with the repo mounted to /upstream . Each agent clones a local copy to /workspace , and when it's done, pushes from its own local container to upstream."
- Claiming: "Claude takes a "lock" on a task by writing a text file to current_tasks/ (e.g., one agent might lock current_tasks/parse_if_statement.txt, while another locks current_tasks/codegen_function_definition.txt). If two agents try to claim the same task, git's synchronization forces the second agent to pick a different one."
- The locks are in git: "In the git repository of the project, you can read through the history and watch it take out locks on various tasks." That backs up "committing" a lock file.

What the page does not support:
1. "Git refused a second claim." The source only says "git's synchronization forces the second agent to pick a different one." It never says how: a rejected push, a merge conflict on pull, or the agent finding the lock file already there. Git refusing is an inference, not a quote. It is also not guaranteed: two identical lock files would merge cleanly. The template's mechanism is different. GitHub rejects a second push to an existing branch `claude/<issue>` as non-fast-forward. That makes the template's claim stricter than a lock file on a shared branch.
2. "Close to this template's protocol." This is true for claiming only. The rest of the workflow is the opposite of this template's PR-gated flow. Each agent integrates straight into the shared upstream with no pull request, no review and no CI gate: "Claude works on the task, then pulls from upstream, merges changes from other agents, pushes its changes, and removes the lock. Merge conflicts are frequent, but Claude is smart enough to figure that out." There is no coordinator either: "I haven't yet implemented any other method for communication between agents, nor do I enforce any process for managing high-level goals. I don't use an orchestration agent."

Corrected statement: In Carlini's C-compiler project (Anthropic Engineering, Feb 5, 2026), 16 Opus 4.6 agents each ran in their own Docker container. Each cloned a shared bare git repo (mounted at /upstream) into /workspace and pushed back to it. An agent claimed a task by writing a lock text file into current_tasks/, which then appears in git history. The source says "git's synchronization forces the second agent to pick a different one", but does not say how. Agents then pulled, merged, pushed their work straight to the shared upstream and removed the lock: no pull requests, no review gate, no orchestrator. The lock-file claim is like this template's claim file (docs/agents/claims/<issue>.md). claims.claim: Concurrent agent PRs (replication package for the 'Concurrent AI-Agent Pull Requests on GitHub' paper, AIDev-pop corpus): pairs of PRs open at the same time by different agents conflicted about twice as often as pairs by the same agent. Mixing agent or model types is therefore a confounder.
corrections:
The numbers are right, but the conclusion drawn from them is not in the source, and the study's own sampling does not support it.

What the source says: the README at raw.githubusercontent.com/Quantum535/concurrent-agentic-prs-replication/HEAD/README.md reads: "Headline numbers derivable from this file: intra-agent 119/601 = 19.8% (95% Wilson CI [16.8, 23.2]); cross-agent 48/115 = 41.7% (95% CI [33.1, 50.9]); 716/747 evaluable (95.8%)." The repo's rq3_rates_full.csv gives the same figures: same,119,601; cross,48,115. So cross-agent co-active pairs conflicted about 2.1 times as often as same-agent pairs.

What is wrong with the claim:
(1) "Conflicted" means a textual conflict when the two PR heads were replayed with `git merge-tree --write-tree` after the fact. It does not mean a conflict anyone saw in practice.
(2) The "agents" are products, not models. The CSV lists Claude_Code, Copilot, Cursor, Devin and OpenAI_Codex. The README says nothing about model types.
(3) The README never says that mixing agents is a confounder, and the sampling does not let you blame the gap on mixing. build_sample.py takes the cross stratum only from repos with at least two distinct agents ("we take ALL available cross repos", 122 of them, which its docstring says is all that exist). The intra stratum is a random 625 drawn from any repo with a same-agent pair (seed=42). Each stratum uses one pair per repo: the first overlapping pair found. So the two strata come from different kinds of repo, and the 2x gap may reflect repo selection rather than the agent mix.
(4) The conflict rate also varies by agent within the same-agent stratum (my tally of rq3_merge_replay_full.csv): Devin 31/87 (35.6%), Cursor 11/41 (26.8%), Copilot 38/213 (17.8%), Claude Code 3/18 (16.7%), Codex 36/242 (14.9%). Which agent was used matters on its own, apart from whether agents were mixed.

Correct statement: in the AIDev-pop merge replay, cross-agent co-active PR pairs had a textual conflict rate of 41.7% (48/115) against 19.8% (119/601) for same-agent pairs. The README does not claim this is caused by mixing agents. The cross stratum is limited to the 122 repos that use several agents, and conflict rates differ by agent even within same-agent pairs. For an experiment design, the safe takeaway is to hold the agent product, and the model, fixed across arms as a possible confounder. This study shows the two are associated; it does not show that mixing agents causes conflicts. (Minor: the README says 25 of 747 pairs were unavailable, but rq3_rates_full.csv lists 31, which matches 747 - 716.)

claims.claim: Nool benchmark (vendor-run, pre-registered, small number of repeats): with 25 to 35 concurrent agents on one repo, plain git with good scheduling landed essentially all tickets cleanly when each agent's planned file set was accurate. Coordination tooling only helped when those plans were wrong.

corrections:
Partly wrong; load_bearing. The quote is exact (README.md, "In plain terms", lines 26-30): "When every agent knows exactly which files it's about to touch, Nool and a well-scheduled git setup perform about the same -- both land essentially 100% of tickets cleanly." "Vendor-run" and "pre-registered" are also right: "this is a vendor-run evaluation, pre-registered to mitigate that". Three parts of the claim go beyond what the source says.

(1) The agent counts are wrong. "25 to 35" is the range for a different comparison: Finding 1 sets uncoordinated git (git_fleet) against Nool. The source gives the scheduled-git result at N=10, N=20 and N=35, never at N=25:
- N=10: "git_scheduled | 60/60, 60/60 | 0" (findings report 6a).
- N=20: the zero-noise footprint-noise cells (README: "N=20, corpus v3.1, 2 reps/cell").
- N=35: corpus v3.1 "git_scheduled (3 reps, 60/59/59 of 60, zero conflicts)". On the original v3 corpus the N=35 git-side reps are "still deferred" ("git_scheduled 2/5").

(2) "Cleanly" and "the planned file set" both overstate the result.
- One of the two zero-noise git_scheduled runs is not clean: "rep 1's zero-noise `git_scheduled` run hit 16 broken-main events and a failed final smoke test despite 60/60 accepted". The cause is a billing-ticket cluster in the task set, not the noise treatment. Even so, a footprint that is accurate at file level "can correctly serialize tickets by *time* and still fail to prevent a *semantic* composition defect".
- The accurate plan is not an agent's own plan. It is an oracle footprint taken from the ticket metadata, with noise injected on purpose; the README calls the arm "an oracle-scheduled git baseline".

(3) "Coordination tooling only helped when plans were wrong" holds only for Nool against a git scheduler running the same logic. It is wrong for coordination in general. Scheduling work by file set before it starts is itself coordination, and it beat uncoordinated git by a wide margin even with accurate plans:
- "the coordinated setup landed **100%** of tickets ... Plain, uncoordinated git lost roughly a third of tickets to conflicts at every size (**62-68%** landed across the 4 runs)".
- The audit attributes this "to coordination *policy* (a scheduler that prevents contention before it happens), not to nool the tool specifically".
- A merge queue with CI gates and no scheduler "does not close the gap".

The Nool-only advantage under bad plans is also weak:
- "only 2 repeated runs per condition"; "suggestive, not conclusive, at n=2, and still correlational".
- The light-noise replication at 5 runs per arm shrank the gap: "3.3pp falls to 2.0pp".
- The gap is "an upper bound conditional on correct identity configuration".

Nool also won some mechanism tests regardless of plan accuracy. The README reports attribution of who changed what: "plain git misattributes up to **56%** of operations at 15 simultaneous writers; Nool: **0%**".

Scope: one synthetic Go corpus of 60 tickets ("The repository currently contains only the synthetic Go corpus"), one pinned model (claude-sonnet-5).

Corrected statement: In Nool's vendor-run, pre-registered benchmark (one synthetic Go repo, 60 tickets, 2-5 runs per cell), a git setup with a footprint scheduler, fed oracle file sets, matched Nool's coordinated arm at N=10, 20 and 35: about 59-60 of 60 tickets accepted with zero conflicts. One such run still broke main. Both coordinated setups beat uncoordinated git (62-68% landed) and a merge queue without a scheduler (about 40/60). Nool's extra lead over scheduled git appeared only when footprints were made noisy, and it is small and early: 2.0-6.7 points.

Partly wrong. I read the README at https://raw.githubusercontent.com/noolinc/nool_long_eval_bench/HEAD/README.md and the findings report it links (docs/findings/2026-08-21-findings.md in the same repository). The quoted sentence is real, and so are "vendor-run" and "pre-registered". The claim goes wrong in four places. All four are load-bearing for an experiment that gates work by declared file sets.

(1) Wrong fleet sizes. The "25 to 35 agents" range comes from finding 1, which compares nool_fleet with uncoordinated git_fleet. The well-scheduled git arm (git_scheduled) was run at different sizes:
- N=10: 60/60 and 60/60.
- N=20: the zero-noise cell of the footprint-noise study (?8d), 2 reps.
- N=35: 3 reps on corpus v3.1 (60/60, 59/60, 59/60). The pre-registered N=35 runs on corpus v3 stopped at 2 of 5 reps: "`git_scheduled` 2/5 -- still deferred".

No git_scheduled run at N=25 is reported. The "plans wrong" comparison was run only at N=20: "N=20, corpus v3.1, 2 reps/cell across 4 noise levels".

(2) "Cleanly" overstates it. The findings report says: "`git_scheduled`'s zero-noise r1 accepted 60/60 with 16 broken-main events and a failed final smoke test ... a materially different outcome from `nool_gated`'s clean 60/60 in the same cell". The report traces this to a corpus cluster built to compose wrongly, not to noise. Still, its own lesson is that "an oracle, file-level footprint can correctly serialize tickets by *time* and still fail to prevent a *semantic* composition defect". So accepted tickets are not the same as a healthy main branch.

(3) "Coordination tooling only helped when plans were wrong" mixes up two results.
- Scheduling before work starts (claim the files, then work) helped a lot in every condition. Uncoordinated git landed "62-68%", and one N=35 run fell to "33%" (20/60). Coordinated runs landed 100%.
- Only Nool the tool, compared with a git scheduler using "the identical check-in logic", showed no edge with accurate plans and an edge with noisy ones.

(4) The noise result is small and early. The gaps are 3.3, 5.0 and 6.7 points. The light-noise replication reached 5 reps "and retains a smaller 2.0-point Nool lead". The report calls the result "suggestive, not conclusive, at n=2". The mechanism "is not directly observed". The gap "should be read as an upper bound conditional on correct identity configuration".

Two further limits:
- The "accurate plans" were oracle footprints supplied by the harness, with noise added on purpose. They were not plans the agents wrote. Real drift was seen once: "the agent edited `service/users.go`, a file outside its declared footprint".
- The study used one model (claude-sonnet-5) on one synthetic Go corpus of 60 tickets.

Correct statement: in Nool's vendor-run, pre-registered study (one model, synthetic Go corpus, 2-5 reps per cell), a git scheduler that admits tickets against oracle file footprints matched Nool's gated arm on accepted tickets (60/60, zero conflicts at N=10; 59-60/60 at N=35). In the N=20 noise study it also matched at 60/60 with zero noise, though one of its two zero-noise runs left main broken. Uncoordinated git lost about a third of tickets. When 10-50% of footprint entries were wrong (N=20 only), Nool led the git scheduler by 3.3 to 6.7 points on 2 reps per cell, and the report calls this suggestive, not conclusive.

Partly wrong. The quote is real and the framing (vendor-run, pre-registered, few repeats) is accurate, but the claim gets the agent counts wrong and misstates what "only helped" refers to. Load-bearing: yes.

Sources opened: README https://raw.githubusercontent.com/noolinc/nool_long_eval_bench/HEAD/README.md and findings report https://raw.githubusercontent.com/noolinc/nool_long_eval_bench/HEAD/docs/findings/2026-08-21-findings.md

What holds:
- README lines 26-28, verbatim: "When every agent knows exactly which files it's about to touch, Nool and a well-scheduled git setup perform about the same -- both land essentially 100% of tickets cleanly."
- README line 490 discloses "this is a vendor-run evaluation, pre-registered to mitigate that".
- The repeat counts are small: "only 2 repeated runs per condition so far".

What is wrong:

1. Agent count. The source does not tie the perfect-plan parity result to 25 to 35 agents. The N=25 and N=35 figures come from finding 1, which compares Nool against uncoordinated git ("Plain, uncoordinated git lost roughly a third of tickets ... 62-68% landed"). The perfect-plan comparison of the coordinated git scheduler (`git_scheduled`) against `nool_gated` was run at these sizes:
   - N=20, the footprint-noise study: "Perfect | 100.0% | 100.0% | 0 pts"; "zero-noise 60/60 both arms".
   - N=10: "git_scheduled | 60/60, 60/60 | 0".
   - N=35: on corpus v3.1, "git_scheduled | v3.1 | 3 | 60/60, 59/60, 59/60 | 0 each". On the original v3 corpus only 2 of the 5 planned reps were run ("git_scheduled at 2/5 -- deferred").
   
   Neither document reports a `git_scheduled` run at N=25.

2. "Coordination tooling only helped when plans were wrong." This is backwards if "coordination" means scheduling. Coordination, meaning the check-in before an agent starts work, helped a great deal even when plans were accurate:
   - Uncoordinated git landed 62-68% of tickets, with one N=35 run at 33%.
   - A CI-gated merge queue with no scheduler, `git_gated_queue`, "does not close the gap -- its accept rate tracks plain git_fleet" (40/60). It also wasted about 38-40% of its spend.
   
   The README credits the win to "the *idea* of checking in before starting work, not specifically from Nool as a tool". Only Nool's edge over an equally scheduled git setup shows up when plans are wrong, and that edge is small and tentative:
   - The gap grew from 0 to 3.3, 5.0 and then 6.7 points at N=20 with 2 reps per cell.
   - At 5 reps, the light-noise replication "retains a smaller 2.0-point Nool lead".
   - The README calls it "not yet a strong claim" and "suggestive, not conclusive, at n=2".
   - It also says the gap "should be read as an upper bound conditional on correct identity configuration".

3. "Cleanly" needs a caveat. In one of the two zero-noise N=20 `git_scheduled` runs, all 60 of 60 tickets were accepted, but there were "16 broken-main events and a failed final smoke test". The findings trace this to a designed billing-file conflict cluster in the ticket corpus, not to the scheduler or the plan noise. Even so, accepted-ticket counts do not show whether the shared main branch stayed healthy.

Corrected statement: In Nool's vendor-run, pre-registered benchmark (60-ticket synthetic Go corpus, claude-sonnet-5, 2 to 5 reps per cell), a git setup with a footprint-gated scheduler matched Nool's coordinated arm (about 100% of tickets landed, zero conflicts) whenever agents' declared file footprints were accurate. This was measured at N=10, N=20 and N=35, not at N=25. Uncoordinated git, and a CI-gated merge queue without upfront scheduling, lost about a third of tickets to conflicts at every size. Nool's own advantage over the scheduled git setup appeared only under injected footprint noise, and it was small and preliminary: 0 to 6.7 points at N=20 with n=2, and a 2.0-point lead at n=5 for light noise.

What this means for the experiment design: in this benchmark, assigning work up front (claiming files before starting) is what avoids conflicts; checking at merge time through PR or CI gates alone does not.

It also says not to interrupt focused work, because "interrupting yourself while coding is actually *more* expensive to the team than making another developer wait a bit for a code review." It cares most about "the *response* time ... as opposed to how long it takes a CL to get through the whole review and be submitted."

Correct statement: Google's code review guide (eng-practices, reviewer/speed.md) says slow reviews lower the velocity of the whole team, harm code health and frustrate developers. It sets a norm of responding within one business day, with several rounds possible in a day. It puts per-response latency ahead of total time to submit, and it accepts a short wait over interrupting a reviewer's focused work. It does not say review latency is the main cost of review gating, and it says nothing about AI reviewers.

Load-bearing: yes. Whether to inject or measure review latency is an experiment-design choice. To mirror Google's norm, a human-like review gate would model latency of up to about one business day per response, not zero. The experiment should measure three things separately: latency per response, the number of re-review rounds (including the author's revision time), and review quality or defects that get through. Treat the idea that an instant AI reviewer removes the cost of gating as a hypothesis to test, not a cited fact.

Cite the scaling-with-agents effect as a hypothesis to measure, not as a documented fact.

Partly wrong. The quoted sentence is in the source, but the source does not support "is the default" without a qualifier, and it says nothing about agents or about cost growing with their number.

What these sources do not settle:
- Whether a merge completed by auto-merge that was switched on with GITHUB_TOKEN fires push workflows on main. Nothing in the docs says; test it.
- The auto-merge pages mention only branch protection rules, never rulesets. Whether a ruleset with required checks also enables auto-merge has to be tested.
- What fromJSON('') does is not documented. A missing variable reads as '', so guard with `vars.X || '[]'`.
- The approval-required runs for GITHUB_TOKEN-made PRs are still rolling out on dotcom, per the feature file. Either way, CI does not start on its own for such PRs.

What follows for the experiment design (my inferences):
- Agent legs should push and open PRs with a GitHub App installation token, for example the main account's own App, or a PAT. Otherwise CI either needs a human approval or never runs, and auto-merge stalls.
- The orchestrator can fan out with GITHUB_TOKEN plus `actions: write` through workflow_dispatch. The dispatched workflow must already be on the default branch. return_run_details=true returns the run ID.
- The matrix can be `fromJSON(vars.ARMS)` with at most 256 legs. On Free, only 20 jobs run at once. Give each leg its own concurrency group built from github.workflow plus a matrix value. Use `queue: max` wherever several dispatches can share one group, or pending runs get cancelled.
- Auto-merge on GitHub Free needs a public repository, 'Allow auto-merge' turned on, and a branch protection rule with a required status check (the 'check' job). Without a required check, `gh pr merge --auto` simply merges at once.
- Strict up-to-date checks, the default, make every merge force rebases elsewhere. That is the coordination cost the experiment measures, and those rebases show up as head_ref_force_pushed in each PR's timeline.
- GITHUB_TOKEN cannot set variables or secrets or change repository settings. Secrets need LibSodium, which Python's standard library lacks, so use `gh secret set`.
- GITHUB_TOKEN's 1,000 requests per hour per repository is shared by every agent.
- Since 2026-10-01, check runs and workflow runs are deleted after the retention period: 90 days by default, and at most 90 on public repositories. Export results promptly; artifact downloads need a token even on public repositories.
- claude-code-action's FAQ says Claude does not rebase or force-push, and its App cannot write workflow files. A 'main moved, rebase' protocol therefore needs a different executor or a custom setup.

corrections:
Partly refuted. The first three sentences are correct: I opened the source at the pinned commit (raw.githubusercontent.com/github/docs/9f651797567230e844373870fce8b14427ad47ad/data/reusables/actions/actions-do-not-trigger-workflows.md), and it matches main word for word. The same file opens by saying events triggered by GITHUB_TOKEN create no workflow run, "with the following exceptions: * `workflow_dispatch` and `repository_dispatch` events always create workflow runs." A user with write access starts them with "Approve workflows to run". Other pull_request activity types create no runs, and other GITHUB_TOKEN events create none either, except workflow_dispatch and repository_dispatch, which always create runs. Partly wrong: the quote and the mechanics are accurate, but the conclusion goes further than the source.

What the source does say. I opened data/reusables/actions/actions-do-not-trigger-workflows.md at commit 9f651797. It is identical on main today, and the quoted sentence is word for word. It says that when a workflow using GITHUB_TOKEN creates or updates a pull request, the resulting pull_request event (opened, synchronize or reopened) creates runs in an "approval-required" state. "a user with write access to the repository can start the runs by selecting **Approve workflows to run**." Other pull_request types (labeled, edited, closed) create no runs.

Where the claim goes too far:

1. "Cannot get CI to run on their own" is too strong. The same file's first exception reads: "`workflow_dispatch` and `repository_dispatch` events always create workflow runs." A GITHUB_TOKEN workflow can still start CI on the PR branch by dispatch, if the CI workflow declares that trigger. Only the pull_request-triggered runs are held for approval.

2. It is narrower than "agents that open PRs". The rule covers only PRs created or updated "by a workflow using GITHUB_TOKEN". PRs pushed or opened with a PAT, a GitHub App installation token or a user's own credentials are not covered by this text.

3. It is not settled or universal. The sentence sits inside `{% ifversion actions-github-token-pull-request-approval %}`. The flag file at the same commit, data/features/actions-github-token-pull-request-approval.yml, sets `fpt: '*'` and `ghec: '*'`, with GHES commented out as "# Uncomment when this ships to GHES (currently rolling out on dotcom)". So it is a change still rolling out on github.com and GHEC, not on GHES. A given repository may still have the older behavior, where those events create no run at all.

The REST approve endpoint (POST /repos/{owner}/{repo}/actions/runs/{run_id}/approve) is documented only for "a pull request from a public fork of a first time contributor". A user with write access must approve them ("Approve workflows to run") before they execute. Other pull_request types triggered that way create no runs. This does not stop such a workflow from starting CI via workflow_dispatch or repository_dispatch, which always create runs. It does not apply to PRs opened or pushed with a non-GITHUB_TOKEN credential (PAT, GitHub App token, user OAuth).

I'm marking this refuted on its last sentence. The first three sentences are right: the quote matches the cited file at commit 9f651797 word for word, and it reads the same on main. Corrected statement (load_bearing):

1. **The new rule.** When a workflow creates or updates a pull request with GITHUB_TOKEN, the resulting `pull_request` event with `opened`, `synchronize` or `reopened` creates workflow runs in an "approval-required" state. Whether such a dispatched run satisfies a required status check on the pull request is not stated in these pages.

corrections:
Partly refuted. The first sentence is correct and the quote is exact. I opened the cited file at commit 9f65179 (raw.githubusercontent.com, line 1150, in the NOTE under "## `workflow_run`"). It reads: "You can't use `workflow_run` to chain together more than three levels of workflows. For example, if you attempt to trigger five workflows (named `B` to `F`) to run sequentially after an initial workflow `A` has run (that is: `A` -> `B` -> `C` -> `D` -> `E` -> `F`), workflows `E` and `F` will not be run." In the example the starting workflow A is not one of the three levels. So A plus three chained levels (B, C, D) run, and only a fourth level or deeper is dropped.

The second sentence, "Fan-out should use dispatch, not workflow_run chains", is not in the source, and it mixes up two different things.
(a) The limit is on how deep a chain goes in sequence, not on how many workflows one event starts. Fan-out under workflow_run is several workflows each naming A in `workflows:`. Each of those is only one level from A, so this note does not limit it.
(b) The source names no alternative to workflow_run chains and never mentions dispatch as a way around the depth limit. It also says nothing about whether dispatch chains have a depth limit of their own.

The nearest primary statement is in a different file at the same commit, data/reusables/actions/actions-do-not-trigger-workflows.md (included in trigger-a-workflow.md under "Triggering a workflow from a workflow"). claude-mechanics.notes:
What I checked: every quote above was matched word for word, by script, against the source it cites. Sources were a clone of anthropics/claude-code-action at 2dca132 (the commit both the v1 and v1.0.247 tags point to, dated 2026-10-08), the code.claude.com docs fetched as .md, support.claude.com articles converted from HTML, and the github/docs source repository.

Source caveat: the sandbox proxy blocks docs.github.com, so the GitHub claims cite the github/docs source files (the reusables and limits.md) that docs.github.com is built from. The text is the same; only the URL differs.

Gaps and inferences:
1. Concurrency (question 3): no primary source gives a cap on concurrent sessions per Pro or Max token. Limits are usage-based only: a five-hour window plus a weekly limit, pooled across every surface and every job using the token, with a "may limit ... at our discretion" clause. GitHub issues report OAuth refresh races when many sessions share one login. Those are not primary sources, and a static CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN does not refresh, so I left them out of the claims.
2. Waiting out a limit in CI: the docs describe waiting for a reset only for interactive sessions. That a -p run fails rather than waits when the plan quota runs out is an inference from that wording plus the 429 retry rules, which cover throttles "that don't carry your plan's quota headers".
3. CLAUDE_CODE_RETRY_WATCHDOG: action.yml has a comment saying the step's env block shadows job-level env for the variables it lists. I did not test this. The safe way to get the variable to the CLI is the action's `settings` input with an "env" block.
4. Cross-job messaging: "Actions jobs cannot message each other" is derived from two quotes. Runners are separate machines, and setup-token cannot set up Remote Control.

Design implications:
- Measure each run from the result entry of execution_file: modelUsage tokens (which include subagents), num_turns, duration_ms. Upload the file with if: always() before the job ends. Do not use total_cost_usd as cost; it is a client-side estimate.
- Pin the action to a SHA, because the CLI version moves with @v1. In claude_args, set --model, --effort, --max-turns, --permission-mode, --allowedTools and, if needed, --setting-sources. Make sure ANTHROPIC_API_KEY and ANTHROPIC_MODEL are absent.
- Leave github_token out so pushes and PRs come from the Claude App and trigger CI. Grant id-token: write. Set allowed_bots for any chained workflow that claude[bot] events trigger.
- Tag mode does not honour the claude/<issue> claim: when the name exists it falls back to a timestamped branch. A PR-gated arm should use automation mode with an explicit prompt and allow gh pr create.
- Arms that share one token compete for one quota. Interleave or randomise arm order, or give each arm its own account's token. Log rate_limit_event utilization from the execution file.
- The native "shared project" form, agent teams, cannot run in Actions because it needs an interactive session and stays on one machine. In CI the only native shared-context forms are subagents and dynamic workflows inside a single session. A teams arm would have to run interactively on one machine, which differs from the Actions arms in environment.

Smaller observations:
- The display_report input defaults to "false" and the code skips the step summary only when it equals "false", so by default no step summary is written.
- As of this commit the action's own install pins Claude Code 2.1.295.

Local copies of the sources are under /tmp/claude-0/-home-user/77769838-64f0-552d-bb56-bbd9b59ae6b6/scratchpad/ (cca/ for the clone, docs/ for the fetched pages).

claims.claim: The message stream (and so execution_file) can include rate_limit_event messages with status, resetsAt and utilization. They can be used to measure how much of the subscription window each run used.

The mode depends on the prompt input. With no prompt, the action is in interactive (@claude) mode and posts its reply as a comment. With a prompt, it is in automation mode: it runs without a mention, and its results go to the run log, not a comment.
claims.quote: * **Automation mode**: when the workflow provides a `prompt` input, Claude runs without waiting for a mention, subject only to the [checks on who can trigger runs](#who-can-trigger-runs). By default, results appear in the workflow run log rather than a comment.

claims.claim: Tag (@claude) mode adds --permission-mode acceptEdits and a fixed tool list itself. Automation (agent) mode adds neither and installs no GitHub MCP servers unless claude_args names their tools. An automation arm has to pass its own --permission-mode and --allowedTools.
claims.quote: claudeArgs += ` --permission-mode acceptEdits --allowedTools "${tagModeTools.join(",")}"`;

claims.claim: The permission mode a -p or Agent SDK session starts in depends on whether the session fetches feature flags: 'default' or 'auto'. Passing --permission-mode explicitly removes this variable between arms.
claims.quote: | `claude -p` or the [Agent SDK](/docs/en/agent-sdk/permissions#permission-modes) | `default` in sessions that [fetch feature flags](/docs/en/env-vars#features-that-need-feature-flag-fetching). In sessions that don't, such as on a third-party provider or with telemetry off, `auto` with Claude Code v2.1.285 or later and `default` on earlier versions.

claims.claim: In tag mode the action makes its own branch, by default {{prefix}}{{entityType}}-{{entityNumber}}-{{timestamp}}. If a branch_name_template produces a name that already exists, it quietly switches to the default timestamped name. So tag mode does not respect an existing claude/<issue> claim branch.
claims.quote: `Branch '${newBranch}' already exists, falling back to default format`,

claims.claim: By default (tag mode) Claude does not open pull requests. It pushes a branch and links to a prefilled PR page, so a PR-gated arm has to open the PR itself (for example by allowing Bash(gh pr create:*) in automation mode).
claims.quote: Claude doesn't create PRs by default. Instead, it pushes commits to a branch and provides a link to a pre-filled PR submission page.

claims.claim: How the action picks its GitHub token: if the github_token input is set, it uses it as given (GITHUB_TOKEN, a PAT or a custom app token). If not, it trades the workflow's OIDC token at api.anthropic.com for a Claude GitHub App installation token.
claims.quote: console.log("Using provided GITHUB_TOKEN for authentication"); ... "https://api.anthropic.com/api/github/github-app-token-exchange",

claims.claim: That one token is used for git pushes, because the action rewrites origin to an x-access-token URL. It is also exported as GITHUB_TOKEN and GH_TOKEN, so any gh pr create Claude runs uses the same identity.
claims.quote: const remoteUrl = `https://x-access-token:${githubToken}@${serverUrl.host}/${context.repository.owner}/${context.repository.repo}.git`;

claims.claim: The Claude GitHub App path needs id-token: write in the workflow permissions.
claims.quote: If you're using the default GitHub App authentication, you must add the `id-token: write` permission to your workflow:

claims.claim: Events made with GITHUB_TOKEN do not start new workflow runs. The exceptions: dispatch events, and pull_request opened/synchronize/reopened, which start runs that wait for approval. If Claude pushes or opens PRs with GITHUB_TOKEN, CI will not run on its own. Use the App token or a custom app token.
claims.quote: When you use the repository's `GITHUB_TOKEN` to perform tasks, events triggered by the `GITHUB_TOKEN` will not create a new workflow run, with the following exceptions:

claims.claim: Anthropic's own docs give the fix: leave out github_token so the action authenticates as the Claude GitHub App, or pass a custom app token.
claims.quote: * GitHub doesn't trigger workflows on commits made with the default `GITHUB_TOKEN`. If you pass `github_token: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}` to the Claude Code GitHub Action, remove it so it authenticates as the Claude GitHub App, or pass a custom app token instead

claims.claim: The action refuses bot actors on every event, scheduled runs included, unless the bot is listed in allowed_bots. A chained workflow fired by claude[bot] activity (for example a review job on a PR Claude opened) needs allowed_bots.
claims.quote: This check also applies to scheduled runs, which GitHub attributes to a repository user, usually the one who last changed the workflow's `cron` schedule. If that user is a bot, list it in `allowed_bots`.

claims.claim: The Claude App token cannot write workflow files. Its default permissions are contents, pull_requests and issues write.
claims.quote: The GitHub App for Claude doesn't have workflow write access for security reasons.

claims.claim: Pro and Max both have a five-hour session limit and a weekly limit. Claude and Claude Code share them, so every Actions job on one subscription token draws from the same pool.
claims.quote: Both Pro and Max plans have a five-hour session limit and a weekly limit. Max plans also have a separate weekly limit for Fable. These limits are shared across Claude and Claude Code, meaning all activity in both tools counts against the same limits.

claims.claim: Usage from all surfaces (claude.ai, Claude Code, Desktop) counts toward the same limit. Interactive use on the same account during an experiment eats into the same budget.
claims.quote: Note that your usage of all different Claude product surfaces (claude.ai, Claude Code, Claude Desktop) counts towards the same usage limit.

claims.claim: Each request counts against the session and weekly allowances at once. A burst of parallel fan-out can use up the weekly allowance before the five-hour window resets.
claims.quote: Usage counts against the session and weekly allowances at the same time. A single burst of heavy activity, such as a large workflow fanout, can exhaust the weekly allowance before the session window resets.

claims.claim: When a session or weekly limit runs out, Claude Code blocks requests until the reset. Switching models does not help. Waiting through the reset is described only for interactive sessions, so a CI run that hits the limit ends instead of pausing.
claims.quote: Claude Code blocks further requests until the reset time shown in the message. The session and weekly limits are shared across all models, so switching models doesn't restore access.

claims.claim: Short-lived 429 throttles are retried automatically, up to 10 times with exponential backoff. For subscription sign-ins this covers 429s that carry no plan-quota headers, meaning throttles rather than an exhausted plan.
claims.quote:
* Temporary 429 throttles, but not a gateway's spend-limit `429`, which isn't a throttle; see [Spend limit reached](#spend-limit-reached).
  * When you're signed in with a claude.ai subscription, this includes 429 throttles that don't carry your plan's quota headers.

claims.claim: In CI, CLAUDE_CODE_RETRY_WATCHDOG=1 makes 429 and 529 capacity errors retry forever instead of failing. That stretches wall-clock time, so a time-to-merge metric has to treat throttle waits as a confound.
claims.quote: Set to `1` in unattended sessions such as CI jobs to retry `429` and `529` capacity errors indefinitely instead of failing after `CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_RETRIES` attempts.

claims.claim: No official page states a cap on concurrent sessions per Pro or Max subscription. The limits are usage windows, and Anthropic says it may add other limits at its discretion.
claims.quote: In addition, to manage capacity and ensure fair access to all users, we may limit your usage in other ways, such as weekly and monthly caps or model and feature usage, at our discretion.

claims.claim: A CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN belongs to the subscription of whoever ran claude setup-token. Arms that share one token share one quota; arms on different accounts have separate quotas.
claims.quote: since an OAuth token is tied to the subscription of the person who ran `claude setup-token`.

claims.claim: setup-token issues a one-year token that can only make model requests. It cannot set up Remote Control, so Actions jobs on separate runners cannot use cross-machine session messaging.
claims.quote: It can only make model requests, so it can't establish [Remote Control](/docs/en/remote-control) sessions or fetch [claude.ai connectors](/docs/en/mcp#use-mcp-servers-from-claude-ai).

claims.claim: ANTHROPIC_API_KEY takes precedence over CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN. If an API key is also present, an arm silently runs on API billing.
claims.quote: 3. `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` environment variable.

claims.claim: GitHub-hosted runners limit concurrent jobs per account plan: 20 on Free, 40 on Pro. That caps how many arms or agents can run in parallel.
claims.quote: | Standard {% data variables.product.github %}-hosted runner | Free | 20 | 5 | Not applicable |

claims.claim: A GitHub-hosted job can run for at most 6 hours.
claims.quote: Each job in a workflow can run for up to 6 hours of execution time.

claims.claim: --max-turns caps agentic turns in print/SDK mode, has no limit by default, and exits with an error when reached.
claims.quote: | `--max-turns` | Limit the number of agentic turns (print mode only). Exits with an error when the limit is reached. No limit by default.

claims.claim: The action takes --model and --max-turns out of claude_args and puts them into SDK options; every other flag (such as --effort, --permission-mode, --setting-sources) passes straight through. A model set by the ANTHROPIC_MODEL env var takes precedence over --model in claude_args, so for equal arms leave ANTHROPIC_MODEL unset.
claims.quote: model: options.model || modelFromClaudeArgs,

claims.claim: With no --model, the action uses Claude Code's default model, which is Opus 5.5 on Pro and Max. Arms should pin --model, because the default changes as releases come out.
claims.quote: * **Pro, Max, Team, Enterprise, and Anthropic API**: defaults to Opus 5.5

claims.claim: Effort also depends on model and settings: Opus 5.5 defaults to medium, and settings files can change it. Pass --effort explicitly so it stays the same across arms.
claims.quote: except that Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, and Haiku 5.5 default to `medium`

claims.claim: By default the action loads user, project and local settings, so the repo's CLAUDE.md and .claude/ settings shape every run. --setting-sources overrides this. Arms that use different repo configurations are not under equal conditions unless that difference is the treatment.
claims.quote: : ["user", "project", "local"],

claims.claim: Each action release pins one Claude Code CLI version: v1.0.247 (the current v1 tag and main) installs 2.1.295, and v1.0.246 installed 2.1.294. Referencing @v1 lets the CLI change in the middle of an experiment, so pin the action to a commit SHA.
claims.quote: const claudeCodeVersion = "2.1.295";

claims.claim: --max-budget-usd is checked against the client-side cost estimate and counts subagent spend. It works as a rough cap but is not exact.
claims.quote: Claude Code checks the cap against its [client-side cost estimate](/docs/en/agent-sdk/cost-tracking#estimates-not-billing), which can differ from your bill. Spend from [subagents](/docs/en/sub-agents) counts toward the cap.

claims.claim: --fallback-model swaps in another model when the main one is overloaded. Leave it unset if arms must stay on one model.
claims.quote: Enable automatic fallback to the specified model(s) when the primary model is overloaded or not available

claims.claim: Claude Code has a native agent teams feature: a lead session, teammates, a shared task list and a mailbox. It is experimental, off by default, and turned on with CLAUDE_CODE_EXPERIMENTAL_AGENT_TEAMS=1.
claims.quote: Agent teams are experimental and disabled by default. Enable them by setting `CLAUDE_CODE_EXPERIMENTAL_AGENT_TEAMS=1`

claims.claim: Agent teams do not work in -p or Agent SDK sessions, which is how claude-code-action runs. A team-based 'shared project' arm cannot run inside GitHub Actions and needs an interactive session.
claims.quote: Spawning teammates also requires an interactive session. In [non-interactive mode](/docs/en/headless) with the `-p` flag, including Agent SDK sessions, Claude doesn't spawn teammates, and a subagent that Claude names runs as an ordinary [subagent](/docs/en/sub-agents) even with agent teams enabled.

claims.claim: A team belongs to one session on one machine (its config and tasks live under ~/.claude/teams and ~/.claude/tasks) and cannot be shared across sessions.
claims.quote: * **One team per session**: a session has exactly one team, scoped to that session. You can't create additional named teams or share a team across sessions.

claims.claim: Anthropic's docs say agent teams add coordination overhead and use many more tokens, and that teammates editing the same file overwrite each other. This is a vendor-documented cost of the shared-collaboration form.
claims.quote: Agent teams add coordination overhead and use significantly more tokens than a single session.

claims.claim: Subagents do work in -p/SDK sessions. Each has its own context window, and its requests count against the same usage limits. In-session delegation in CI therefore has to use subagents (or dynamic workflows), not teams.
claims.quote: It also sends its own requests, which count toward the same [usage limits](/docs/en/costs#plan-usage-breakdown) as your main conversation.

claims.claim: Dynamic workflows (scripts that orchestrate many subagents) are available in claude -p and the Agent SDK.
claims.quote: Workflows are available in the CLI, the Desktop app, the IDE extensions, [non-interactive mode](/docs/en/headless) with `claude -p`, and the [Agent SDK](/docs/en/agent-sdk/overview).

claims.claim: Messaging between sessions is local unless Remote Control is involved. Reaching sessions on other machines needs Remote Control with a claude.ai sign-in, which a setup-token cannot provide. Separate Actions jobs cannot message each other natively.
claims.quote: Claude finds your [cloud sessions](/docs/en/claude-code-on-the-web) and your sessions on other machines from a session that is connected to Remote Control, which needs a claude.ai sign-in as this session's active authentication
